title: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 10 Minutes
description:
From a legend about twins and a wolf in 753 BC to a boy emperor quietly retired in 476 AD, this is the whole story of Rome in about ten minutes: kings, a republic, Hannibal's elephants, Caesar and the pirates, an emperor who taxed pee, and the day the empire was sold at auction. Every fact is checked against ancient writers and modern historians, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #rome #romanempire #juliuscaesar #animatedhistory

beats.say: March, 193 AD. The Roman Empire, the most powerful state on Earth, is about to be sold. At an auction.
The Praetorian Guard, the emperor's own bodyguards, have just killed the emperor Pertinax. Now they're taking bids.
Who wants to be emperor? Bids per soldier, please!
Twenty thousand sesterces each!
Twenty-five thousand! Right now!
Sesterces were Roman coins. And that price was for every single guard.
Sold!
Spoiler: this did not go well for him. So how did the greatest empire on Earth end up for sale? Let's go back. Way back.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 10 Minutes

show.title: A Wolf, Twins and a City

beats.say: Rome began as a few hills next to a river called the Tiber, in the middle of Italy.
Roman legend says twin brothers, Romulus and Remus, were abandoned as babies and raised by a she-wolf.
Which, sure. Totally normal childhood.
When they grew up, they wanted to build a city, but they couldn't agree on which hill.
The Aventine hill. Obviously.
The Palatine hill. Obviously!
In the most famous version, Romulus killed his brother and named the city after himself. Rome.
Later Romans counted April twenty-first, 753 BC, as Rome's birthday. Archaeologists say people lived there even earlier, but a wolf is a better story.

show.label: Rome's traditional birthday
show.sub: April 21, worked out by Romans centuries later

beats.say: At first, Rome was ruled by kings. Tradition says there were seven, and the last was Tarquin the Proud. The nickname tells you how that went.
Around 509 BC, the Romans threw Tarquin out and swore they'd never have a king again.
Instead, they elected two leaders called consuls, each for just one year. Two bosses, so neither could get too powerful.
This was the Roman Republic: no king, just elected leaders and a senate, a council of rich and powerful men. Its symbol was four letters, SPQR, the Senate and People of Rome.

show.label: THE ROMAN REPUBLIC
show.sub: SPQR: the Senate and People of Rome

beats.say: Then, around 387 BC, an army of Gauls, warrior tribes from the north, beat the Romans and captured the city.
The Romans agreed to pay a thousand pounds of gold to make them leave. When they complained the Gauls' weights were rigged, Brennus threw his sword onto the scale too.
And according to the Roman historian Livy, he said this.

show.who: Brennus, as told by Livy, History of Rome 5.48

beats.say: Rome never forgot that. Over the next century or so, it fought and conquered its way across most of Italy.
Next, Rome ran into Carthage, a rich trading city in North Africa. The two fought three wars, called the Punic Wars.
Carthage had the strongest navy around, and Rome barely had one. So, says the Greek historian Polybius, the Romans copied a wrecked Carthaginian warship and built about a hundred of their own.
In the second war, a Carthaginian general named Hannibal had a truly wild idea.
What if we attack Italy... from the top?
Over the Alps? With elephants?
Especially with elephants.
In 218 BC, he marched out of Spain, over the Pyrenees mountains, across the Rhone river and up into the Alps, with thousands of soldiers and thirty-seven war elephants.
Snow, cliffs, landslides, angry mountain tribes. Britannica says that on the fifteenth day he came down into Italy, with most of those elephants still alive.
Fun fact: historians still argue about which mountain pass he used.
Then, in 216 BC at Cannae in southern Italy, he crushed a huge Roman army.
Ancient writers put the Roman losses at somewhere between about fifty and seventy thousand men.

show.label: Roman soldiers lost at Cannae (ancient estimates)
show.sub: ancient writers say 50,000 to 70,000, in a single day

beats.say: But Rome refused to quit. It kept raising new armies, and Hannibal spent about fifteen years in Italy without ever taking the city.
In 202 BC, the Roman general Scipio finally beat him at Zama in Africa, and in 146 BC Rome destroyed Carthage completely.
Rome now ruled the Mediterranean. And with no big enemy left, the Romans started fighting each other.

show.title: Caesar and the Ides of March

beats.say: Enter the most famous Roman of all: Julius Caesar, a politician and general.
Around 75 BC, young Caesar was sailing to the Greek island of Rhodes when pirates captured him.
We're holding you for twenty talents of silver!
Twenty? Do you know who I am? Ask for fifty.
According to Plutarch, a Greek writer, Caesar was held for thirty-eight days, bossed the pirates around, and read them his poems.
Quiet, I'm napping. And one day I'll have you all executed.
They laughed. Once the ransom was paid, he raised a fleet, caught them, and kept his promise.
Grown-up Caesar conquered Gaul, which is basically modern France. Then in 49 BC he led his army into Italy and won a civil war.
After one very quick war in the east, his victory parade carried a sign with just three words: I came, I saw, I conquered.
Then the senate named him dictator for life. A lot of senators hated the 'for life' part.
On the Ides of March, which means March fifteenth, 44 BC, a group of senators, including his friend Brutus, stabbed him to death at a senate meeting.
And he probably never said 'Et tu, Brute?' That line comes from Shakespeare, sixteen hundred years later.
Killing Caesar didn't save the republic. It started even more civil wars.
The winner was Caesar's adopted son, Octavian. In 31 BC, his fleet beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt, at the sea battle of Actium.
Antony and Cleopatra fled back to Egypt, and the war was basically over.
In 27 BC, the senate gave him a shiny new name: Augustus. He said he had restored the republic. Really, he had become Rome's first emperor.
Emperor? Me? No, no. I'm just the first citizen.
He ruled for about forty years, the month of August is named after him, and he rebuilt so much that his biographer made this famous claim.

show.text: He could justly boast that he had found it built of brick and left it in marble.

beats.say: Later, an emperor named Vespasian, who started building the Colosseum, needed money. Fast.
So he taxed the urine collected from public toilets, which people used for laundry and for tanning leather.
Dad. A tax on pee? That's disgusting.
Smell this coin. Does it stink?
No?
And yet it comes from urine.
That story comes from Suetonius, a Roman biographer, and it gave us the saying 'money doesn't stink'.

show.label: A Latin saying born from a pee tax

beats.say: By 117 AD, under the soldier emperor Trajan, the empire reached its biggest size ever.
It stretched from northern Britain to Egypt, and from Portugal to Mesopotamia, which is modern Iraq.
That's roughly five million square kilometres, about half the size of the United States, all ruled from one city.

show.label: Roman Empire in 117 AD
show.sub: about half the size of the USA

beats.say: And Rome itself may have had around a million people. No city in Europe matched that again until London, around 1800.

show.label: People living in Rome (estimate)
show.sub: no European city matched it until London, about 1800

beats.say: Roman concrete was so good that the Pantheon, a temple rebuilt by the next emperor, Hadrian, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
It has been a church since 609, and it's still in use today.
Then things went downhill. The emperor Commodus loved fighting as a gladiator in the arena.
The senator and historian Cassius Dio says Commodus paid himself a million sesterces for every day he fought.
He was murdered in 192. The next emperor, Pertinax, lasted just eighty-seven days before his own guards killed him.
And then came our auction. Here's how Dio, who was in Rome at the time, described it.

show.text: Just as if it had been in some market or auction-room, both the City and its entire empire were auctioned off.

beats.say: But generals out in the provinces had armies too, and one of them, Septimius Severus, marched on Rome.
After just sixty-six days on the throne, Julianus was killed in the palace. Buddy, you bought an empire at a yard sale.
And it got messier. Between 235 and 284 AD, at least twenty-six men claimed to be emperor.
Then came Constantine, the first Roman emperor to become a Christian. In 330, he moved the capital east to a new city he named after himself: Constantinople, today's Istanbul.
Naming a city after yourself? Romulus would be proud.
By 395, the empire was run as two halves, east and west, each with its own emperor. Only the west was in real trouble.
In 410, Alaric and the Visigoths, a Germanic people, looted Rome for three days. It was the first time in almost eight hundred years a foreign enemy had taken the city.
The western emperor, Honorius, was safe far away in Ravenna, and there's a famous story about how he took the news.
Emperor! Roma has perished!
What? But she was eating out of my hand just now!
Not your chicken, sir. The city.
That story, about a pet chicken named Roma, comes from the historian Procopius, and it's almost certainly made up. But it tells you what people thought of Honorius.
Finally, in 476, a Germanic general named Odoacer took power in Italy and removed the boy usually counted as the last western emperor, Romulus Augustus.
People called him Augustulus, 'little Augustus'. And yes, his name mixed Rome's founder and its first emperor. History has jokes.
Keep your pension, kid. I'll just be King of Italy.
Odoacer didn't even call himself emperor. He sent the boy to retire on a pension at a fortress near Naples, where he may have lived for decades.
So is that the end of Rome? Not exactly. The eastern half still called itself the Roman Empire, and it kept going until 1453.
From a wolf legend to a boy emperor, that's more than twelve hundred years. Not bad for a village on a few hills.
If Rome's wars felt ridiculous, wait until you see our next video: the most ridiculous wars in history. See you there.
